{
  "title": "Error-Taxonomy-Guided Curriculum for Self-Improving Reasoning via Diagnostic Co-Evolution",
  "core_problem": "Can a PRM serving as a co-evolving diagnostic instrument—classifying step-level reasoning failures into an evolving error taxonomy and feeding a bandit-based curriculum allocator—drive more efficient self-improvement than instance-level weakness targeting (Socratic-Zero), concept-level weakness extraction (SwS), scalar uncertainty targeting (R-Zero), embedding-diversity coverage (Prism), or multi-agent quality filtering (SAGE), and does tracking error-type distribution dynamics across iterations yield predictive signals for convergence and curriculum collapse?",
  "opportunity": "Self-improving reasoning loops have proliferated rapidly, with 25–30 directly relevant papers in the last 12 months alone (ICLR 2026 RSI Workshop accepted 110 papers). Yet despite this activity, every existing framework diagnoses weaknesses at a granularity that is either too coarse or unstructured to support targeted remediation. Socratic-Zero (Sep 2025) achieves +15.4pp via Teacher-generated problems from individual failed solutions but performs instance-level targeting without aggregating error patterns—it cannot detect that 40% of algebra failures stem from sign errors vs. 60% from conceptual gaps. SwS (NeurIPS 2025) achieves 10%/7.7% gains via concept-level weakness identification but conflates distinct failure modes under shared topic labels. R-Zero (ICLR 2026) achieves +6.49 via uncertainty-based co-evolution but its curriculum signal is purely scalar (p̂ ≈ 0.5). SAGE (March 2026) implements 4-agent co-evolution where the Critic scores quality but not error type—it is a filter, not a diagnoser. WarriorMath (Aug 2025) claims 'defect-aware' synthesis but operationalizes defects as binary pass/fail across 16 rollouts. Prism (March 2026) preserves embedding-space diversity but not diagnostic diversity. Meanwhile, the analytical tools exist but remain disconnected from curriculum design: LEMMA (ACL 2025) defines 7 error types for static SFT; Error Classification of LLMs on MWP (EMNLP 2025) discovers 39 dynamic error clusters but uses them only for inference-time prompting; ErrorMap (Jan 2026) builds hierarchical error taxonomies with 95.2% coverage but applies them only for evaluation. The untapped synthesis: use a PRM as a co-evolving diagnostic instrument whose step-level error-type classifications feed a bandit-based curriculum allocator that optimizes learning gain per error category, while tracking error-type distribution dynamics to predict convergence and detect curriculum collapse before it occurs. Two problems may share the same concept (algebra), difficulty level, and even the same error instance pattern yet fail for structurally different reasons (sign propagation error vs. domain restriction oversight)—only error-type-level diagnosis with aggregated statistics can detect these systematic patterns and allocate training resources accordingly. The Self-Evolving Curriculum (SEC, Bengio group, 2025) demonstrates that bandit-based allocation over problem categories yields +13–33% gains over random allocation, but operates on difficulty levels, not error types. Combining MAB allocation with error-type categories would optimize for learning gain per error category—automatically deprioritizing error types that are already being fixed (diminishing returns) or currently too hard (low returns), and upweighting the most learnable weaknesses at each iteration.",
  "landscape": "**Primary co-evolution baselines:** R-Zero (ICLR 2026) achieves +6.49 (Qwen3-4B) via GRPO-trained challenger targeting p̂ = 0.5 uncertainty, but pseudo-label accuracy degrades from 79% to 63% across iterations and the curriculum signal is purely scalar difficulty. Socratic-Zero (arXiv:2509.24726, Sep 2025) achieves +15.4pp (Qwen3-8B) via Teacher-Solver-Generator co-evolution where the Teacher crafts new problems from individual failed solutions using zone-adaptive generation (Gaussian utility centered at 50% success rate); however, it performs instance-level targeting without error taxonomy or step-level diagnosis—it cannot aggregate error patterns across failures or detect systematic weaknesses. SAGE (arXiv:2603.15255, March 2026) implements 4-agent co-evolution (Challenger/Planner/Solver/Critic) with Task-Relative REINFORCE++ achieving +8.9% on LiveCodeBench and +10.7% on OlympiadBench (Qwen-2.5-7B), but the Critic is a quality filter (scores clarity/relevance on a 1–10 scale), not an error diagnoser—weakness detection is purely implicit through difficulty rewards with no error categorization. WarriorMath (arXiv:2508.01245, Aug 2025) implements 'defect-aware' synthesis with a 5-model expert committee and iterative DPO (36.7%→48.3% on AIME'24 across 3 iterations), but operationalizes defects as binary pass/fail across 16 rollouts with no formal error taxonomy despite the title's implication.\n\n**Weakness-driven synthesis (non-co-evolutionary):** SwS (NeurIPS 2025) achieves 10%/7.7% average gains (Qwen2.5-7B/32B) via outcome-level weakness identification → concept extraction → concept recombination → filtered problem generation; single-round, no PRM, cannot distinguish failures sharing the same topic but differing in error pattern.\n\n**Diversity and curriculum:** Prism (March 2026) addresses R-Zero's diversity collapse via embedding-cluster-based rarity bonuses (+3.98 AMC), but diversity is geometric rather than diagnostic. Vocabulary Dropout (April 2026) injects random token-mask diversity (+4.4 avg on Qwen3-8B) but is blind to what kinds of diversity benefit the solver. Self-Evolving Curriculum (SEC, arXiv:2505.14970, Bengio group) formulates curriculum as multi-armed bandit over problem categories, yielding +13–33% over random allocation via learning-gain-optimized selection; operates on difficulty levels, not error types. Cog-DRIFT (arXiv:2604.04767, April 2026) achieves +10.11% on hard problems via format reformulation (MCQ→cloze→open-ended) with instance-level adaptive progression, but reformulates task format rather than targeting error-type-specific content. Bidirectional Curriculum (arXiv:2603.05120, March 2026) simplifies/complicates problems based on pass/fail signals with a multi-agent framework, but adapts difficulty direction without error taxonomy.\n\n**Error taxonomy and diagnosis:** LEMMA (ACL 2025 Findings, arXiv:2503.17439) defines 7 error types (Calculation/Counting/Formula-Confusion/Question-Misinterpretation/Missing-Step/Confusing-Concept/Nonsensical) for error-type-grounded mistake augmentation in static SFT (~89K examples); closest precursor to error-type-driven training but no curriculum, no co-evolution, no RL. Error Classification of LLMs on MWP (EMNLP 2025 Findings, arXiv:2501.15581) discovers 39 dynamic error clusters via K-means on GPT-4o-analyzed failures and applies Error-Aware Prompting (+26.33% on MATH for Llama-3.1-8B), but uses error knowledge only at inference time, not for training or curriculum. Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (arXiv:2602.06795, Feb 2026) derives 234–296 rubric items per domain with keyword clustering (~50% consolidation), achieving +45% over LLM-as-judge baselines; generates rubrics once without iteration or curriculum design. ErrorMap/ErrorAtlas (arXiv:2601.15812, Jan 2026) builds hierarchical error taxonomies via iterative LLM-based clustering with 95.2% coverage and max 25 categories per level, but applies them only for evaluation. PathFinder-PRM (May 2025) achieves SOTA 67.7 PRMScore with error-aware hierarchical supervision (Mathematical/Consistency/Optimality) but does not use error types for curriculum.\n\n**Verifier co-evolution:** CoVerRL (ACL 2026) demonstrates generator-verifier co-evolution with 4.7–5.9% gains but uses undirected majority voting. VHG (arXiv:2605.06660, May 2026) uses verifier-backed three-party self-play (Setter/Solver/Verifier) to prevent reward hacking in problem generation, improving Pass@1 from 56.8% to 69.0%, but optimizes for difficulty without error diagnosis. RL Tango (NeurIPS 2025) co-trains generator and generative verifier via RL but uses outcome-level rewards. Seirenes (May 2026) implements adversarial self-play with evolving distractions (+7.2 to +10.2pp across scales).\n\n**Other related:** DPE (arXiv:2602.22859, Feb 2026) implements diagnose→generate→retrain for multimodal LLMs using 12 coarse capability dimensions with 4 frontier LLMs but without PRM, step-level analysis, or verifier co-evolution. Self-Error-Instruct (ACL 2025) clusters error keyphrases for targeted data generation but uses GPT-4o and doesn't iterate. R-PRM (NJUNLP 2025) achieves best open-source PRM with fine-grained error categories but does not leverage them for curriculum. APRM (Nov 2025) creates adversarial PRM curriculum (+3.4pp solver accuracy) but targets PRM robustness only. 'GRPO is Secretly a PRM' (Sullivan & Koller, arXiv:2509.21154, Sep 2025; under review at ICML 2026) proves GRPO implicitly performs step-level credit assignment via Monte Carlo estimates from shared token prefixes, clarifying that explicit PRMs add unique value as diagnostic instruments rather than reward signals.\n\n**Positioning summary:** No existing work combines: (a) step-level PRM error-type classification, (b) bandit-based learning-gain-optimized allocation across error categories, (c) hybrid mutation+generation problem synthesis with error-type-validated targeting, (d) iterative co-evolution where the diagnostic instrument itself improves, and (e) predictive analysis of error-type distribution dynamics across iterations.",
  "inspired_by": "Socratic-Zero (2025) validates instance-level weakness targeting via Teacher-Solver-Generator co-evolution but without error taxonomy or pattern aggregation; SwS (NeurIPS 2025) validates weakness-driven synthesis but at concept level; R-Zero (ICLR 2026) validates co-evolutionary self-improvement but with scalar uncertainty; SAGE (2026) validates multi-agent co-evolution but with quality filtering rather than error diagnosis; Prism (2026) validates diversity-aware curriculum but with geographic rather than diagnostic diversity; SEC (2025, Bengio group) validates bandit-based curriculum allocation over problem categories but with difficulty levels rather than error types; LEMMA (ACL 2025) validates error-type-grounded training data construction but in a static single-round SFT setting; Error Classification on MWP (EMNLP 2025) validates dynamic error clustering but only for inference-time prompting; ErrorMap (2026) validates iterative taxonomy construction with 95.2% coverage; Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (2026) validates auto-derived error taxonomies with +45% over LLM-as-judge; 'GRPO is Secretly a PRM' (Sullivan & Koller 2025) establishes that GRPO handles implicit credit assignment, clarifying the PRM's unique value as diagnostic instrument. Field guide Gap 7 (iterative self-improvement loops), Gap 4 (dynamic co-evolution).",
  "approach": "We propose Diagnostic Co-Evolution (DiagCoEvo): a framework where a PRM serves as a co-evolving diagnostic instrument whose step-level error-type classifications feed a bandit-based curriculum allocator, while GRPO with standard outcome rewards handles generator training. We initialize generator and PRM from Qwen3-8B.\n\n**PRM Initialization and Cold-Start Strategy.** Rather than directly applying PathFinder-PRM's taxonomy (trained on Mistral traces + PRM800K), which would face distribution shift to Qwen3-8B, we bootstrap the PRM on the target model's own traces: (i) generate 16 solution attempts per problem from Qwen3-8B on a 3K-problem seed bank; (ii) obtain initial step-level labels via consensus of three signals—Monte Carlo correctness estimation, Math-Verify outcome checking, and LLM-as-judge (Qwen3-72B) analysis; (iii) train the PRM on these Qwen3-8B-native traces with PathFinder-PRM's hierarchical error taxonomy as a seed, augmented with data-driven rubric extraction (inspired by Sanders et al. 2026). The initial taxonomy contains five core types: Mathematical-Computation, Logical-Consistency, Conceptual-Gap, Strategy-Selection, Hallucination.\n\n**Taxonomy Expansion Mechanism.** We adopt a concrete expansion protocol inspired by ErrorMap (2026) and TaxoCom (2022): (i) After each DIAGNOSE phase, errors classified with low PRM confidence (softmax < 0.6) are collected into an 'uncertain' pool. (ii) When the uncertain pool exceeds 5% of recent errors, we apply embedding-based novelty detection: compute cosine distance from each uncertain error's representation to all existing category centroids; errors exceeding a Mahalanobis distance threshold (χ² p < 0.01) are flagged as potential novel types. (iii) Flagged errors are clustered (agglomerative clustering with Ward linkage, silhouette-score-optimal k), and clusters with ≥ 20 instances become candidate new categories. (iv) To prevent explosion, we enforce a hard cap of 12 leaf categories and merge categories whose centroid cosine similarity > 0.85 or whose frequency drops below 2% of total errors for two consecutive iterations. (v) Each expansion/merge event is logged for the error dynamics analysis.\n\n**Each co-evolution iteration executes a four-phase cycle:**\n\n(1) DIAGNOSE: The PRM evaluates the generator's solutions on a held-out problem bank (2K problems, 8 solutions each), classifying each incorrect step's error type to produce a weakness distribution w = {w_1, ..., w_K} over error types. We also extract 'error-triggering contexts'—the problem features and reasoning patterns (e.g., nested negation, multi-variable substitution) most frequently associated with each error type via attention-weighted feature extraction from the PRM's intermediate representations.\n\n(2) GENERATE: Hybrid problem synthesis using a three-tier pipeline ordered by reliability. Tier A (Primary—Problem Mutation, ~50% of budget): Take existing problems the model fails on, apply structured mutations targeting the diagnosed error type—constant perturbation, constraint addition/removal, variable relationship alteration (inspired by Arrows of Math). Mutation preserves problem validity better than generation from scratch. Tier B (Secondary—Weakness-Category-Conditioned Generation, ~35% of budget): The generator produces candidate problems conditioned on error-triggering contexts: 'Generate a problem requiring [operation] in a context where [error-triggering pattern] is likely.' This follows SwS's category-conditioned generation but at error-type rather than concept level. Tier C (Tertiary—Fine-Grained Error-Type Generation, ~15% of budget): Direct type-conditioned prompting for the most specific error types, budgeted conservatively given expected 10–25% yield. All tiers pass through error-type-validated rejection sampling: the generator attempts each candidate (8 rollouts per Tier A/B, 12 per Tier C to compensate for lower yield), the PRM diagnoses the solutions, and we retain only candidates where at least one solution triggers the intended error type. ZPD gating (25–75% solvability) filters gradient-vanishing extremes.\n\n(3) TRAIN GENERATOR: GRPO with outcome-level rewards (Math-Verify for answer correctness). Curriculum allocation uses a multi-armed bandit (MAB) over error-type categories, following SEC's formulation: each error type is one arm, reward = |advantage| from GRPO (measuring immediate learning gain), and selection uses Boltzmann policy over Q-values updated via exponential moving average. This automatically upweights the most learnable error types at each stage—deprioritizing types that are nearly solved (diminishing returns) or currently too hard (low returns). A proportional-allocation floor (minimum 5% sampling rate per active category) ensures coverage of rare-but-important error types, preventing the bandit from ignoring them entirely. Standard GRPO handles implicit step-level credit assignment per Sullivan & Koller (2025). We do NOT use explicit PRM rewards for GRPO, cleanly separating the PRM's diagnostic role from the training objective.\n\n(4) UPDATE DIAGNOSTICIAN: The PRM is retrained on the generator's new trajectories, exposing it to novel error patterns at the generator's current capability frontier. This mirrors R-Zero's frozen-partner scheme: during generator training the PRM is frozen; during PRM update the generator is frozen. After PRM update, the taxonomy expansion mechanism runs to detect emergent error types.\n\n**Experimental Design.** We run 5 iterations, tracking three key dynamics: (a) generator accuracy on MATH-500/AMC/AIME, (b) PRM diagnostic quality on ProcessBench/PRMBench, (c) error-type distribution shift per iteration. Our primary analytical contribution is demonstrating that error-type distributions follow predictable phase transitions during co-evolution (e.g., computational errors resolve first, then logical errors, then strategic errors), and that entropy of the error distribution and per-category learning-gain trajectories provide early-warning signals for convergence plateaus and curriculum collapse—enabling principled stopping criteria.\n\nWe compare against five baselines: (i) Socratic-Zero-style instance-level Teacher targeting (closest structural competitor), (ii) R-Zero-style uncertainty-based co-evolution (scalar difficulty, no error types), (iii) SwS-style concept-level weakness synthesis (single round), (iv) R-Zero + Prism diversity preservation (geographic diversity, no error diagnosis), (v) SEC-style MAB over difficulty levels (bandit allocation without error-type diagnosis). Key ablations: (A) error-type MAB vs. proportional allocation vs. uniform allocation (isolates MAB value); (B) hybrid mutation+generation vs. generation-only (isolates mutation value); (C) PRM co-evolution vs. frozen PRM (isolates diagnostician improvement); (D) dynamic taxonomy expansion vs. fixed 5-type taxonomy (isolates expansion value); (E) number of rejection sampling rollouts (8 vs. 12 vs. 16); (F) tiered generation budget ratios.",

  "description": "We propose Diagnostic Co-Evolution (DiagCoEvo), a framework that repositions the process reward model from a training reward signal to a co-evolving diagnostic instrument for bandit-based curriculum guidance. In a field with 25+ co-evolutionary self-improvement papers in the past year, DiagCoEvo's contribution is both methodological and analytical: methodologically, it uniquely combines step-level PRM error-type classification with MAB-based learning-gain-optimized allocation across error categories and hybrid mutation+generation problem synthesis; analytically, it provides the first characterization of error-type distribution dynamics across multiple co-evolution iterations, yielding predictive signals for convergence and curriculum collapse.\n\nMotivated by Sullivan & Koller (2025, arXiv preprint under review at ICML 2026) showing GRPO already performs implicit step-level credit assignment, we cleanly separate concerns: GRPO with outcome rewards handles generator training, while the PRM's unique value lies in classifying step-level reasoning failures into an evolving error taxonomy that drives curriculum design. The PRM is bootstrapped on the target model's (Qwen3-8B) own traces to avoid cross-model distribution shift, with consensus labeling (MC estimation + Math-Verify + LLM-as-judge) for initialization.\n\nEach iteration executes four phases: (1) DIAGNOSE—PRM evaluates generator solutions, producing an error-type weakness distribution and extracting error-triggering contexts; (2) GENERATE—hybrid three-tier pipeline: problem mutation (50% budget, highest reliability), weakness-category-conditioned generation (35%), and fine-grained type-conditioned generation (15%), all validated via PRM-based error-type rejection sampling with ZPD gating; (3) TRAIN—GRPO with outcome rewards, where curriculum allocation uses a multi-armed bandit over error-type categories (reward = |GRPO advantage|, Boltzmann selection) with a proportional-allocation floor ensuring rare-type coverage; (4) UPDATE—PRM retrained on new trajectories, followed by taxonomy expansion via embedding-based novelty detection with hard cap of 12 leaf categories and automatic merge/split rules.\n\nThis addresses key limitations across the landscape: Socratic-Zero (Sep 2025, +15.4pp) targets weaknesses at instance level without aggregating error patterns or building systematic weakness profiles; SAGE (March 2026) uses a Critic as quality filter rather than error diagnoser; WarriorMath (Aug 2025) operationalizes 'defects' as binary pass/fail; SwS (NeurIPS 2025) diagnoses at concept level; R-Zero (ICLR 2026) targets scalar difficulty; LEMMA (ACL 2025) defines error types but in a static SFT setting without curriculum or co-evolution; SEC (2025) demonstrates MAB curriculum but over difficulty levels, not error types.\n\nOur primary empirical contribution targets +8pp average across MATH-500/AMC/AIME over the strongest baseline, but the primary analytical contribution—showing that error-type distributions follow predictable phase transitions during co-evolution and that per-category learning-gain trajectories provide early-warning signals for convergence—addresses the field's acknowledged gap in theoretical understanding of when and why self-improvement works. We evaluate on Qwen3-8B across 5 iterations against Socratic-Zero, R-Zero, SwS, Prism-augmented, and SEC baselines, with detailed ablations isolating the value of error-type MAB allocation, hybrid generation, PRM co-evolution, and taxonomy expansion.",

    "issue_1_SocraticZero": "ADDRESSED (moderate). Socratic-Zero (arXiv:2509.24726) is now a primary competitor throughout landscape, approach, and baselines. After thorough analysis of the full paper, we position against it precisely: Socratic-Zero's Teacher performs instance-level targeting—generating new problems from individual failed solutions via a refinement function G(q, y_fail)—but never aggregates error patterns into a taxonomy. It cannot detect that 40% of algebra failures stem from sign errors vs. 60% from conceptual gaps because it processes each failure independently. Its verification is binary outcome-level (no PRM, no step-level diagnosis), its difficulty calibration is a scalar Gaussian utility (same as R-Zero's p̂≈0.5), and its Teacher is a frozen 235B oracle rather than a co-evolving diagnostician. DiagCoEvo's error-type-level diagnosis captures systematic patterns that instance-level targeting misses, and its bandit-based allocation optimizes learning gain across error categories rather than treating all failures as equally informative. Socratic-Zero is included as the first baseline (closest structural competitor) in our experimental comparison.",
    "issue_2_SAGE_WarriorMath": "ADDRESSED (moderate). SAGE (arXiv:2603.15255) and WarriorMath (arXiv:2508.01245) are now in the landscape with detailed analysis. SAGE's Critic evaluates question quality (clarity, relevance, well-formedness) on a 1–10 scale but explicitly does NOT determine correctness or diagnose error types—it is a quality filter, not a diagnostic instrument. The Critic cannot distinguish between a Solver failing due to calculation errors vs. conceptual misunderstanding. WarriorMath claims 'defect-aware' but operationalizes defects as binary pass/fail across N=16 rollouts—no formal error categorization exists despite the title. Both papers' key limitation is that weakness detection is implicit through aggregate difficulty/pass-rate signals, whereas DiagCoEvo provides explicit error-type classification enabling targeted remediation.",
    "issue_3_minor_competitors": "ADDRESSED (minor). All five papers now in landscape: LEMMA (ACL 2025 Findings, 7 error types for static SFT), Error Classification of LLMs on MWP (EMNLP 2025 Findings, 39 dynamic clusters for inference-time prompting), Bidirectional Curriculum (March 2026, simplify/complicate on pass/fail), VHG (May 2026, verifier-backed difficulty-focused 3-party self-play), Cog-DRIFT (April 2026, format-based adaptive reformulation). For each, the clear differentiator is provided. LEMMA is the closest precursor (error types + training) but is static/single-round/SFT-only. The Error Classification paper's 39-cluster approach validates dynamic taxonomy discovery but applies it only at inference time. These gaps collectively motivate DiagCoEvo's unique combination of error-type diagnosis + iterative co-evolution + curriculum design.",
    "issue_4_type_conditioned_prompting": "ADDRESSED (highest-risk component, major specification). Based on thorough research, we acknowledge that no paper reports direct success rates for error-type-conditioned generation, and converging evidence suggests 10–25% yield for fine-grained conditioning. We replace the single-strategy generation with a hybrid three-tier pipeline ordered by reliability: Tier A—Problem Mutation (~50% budget): structured mutations of existing failed problems (constant perturbation, constraint addition/removal, variable alteration), inspired by Arrows of Math (2025), which achieves high validity preservation. Tier B—Category-Conditioned Generation (~35%): generation conditioned on error-triggering contexts at moderate specificity, following SwS's approach at error-type rather than concept level. Tier C—Fine-Grained Type-Conditioned Generation (~15%): direct type-conditioned prompting, budgeted conservatively with 12 rollouts per candidate (vs. 8 for Tiers A/B) to compensate for lower yield. All tiers share the PRM-based error-type-validated rejection sampling. Consider adding Actor-Curator as a baseline. (2) **Address REASONMAXXER's policy-selection finding**: Argue that even if RL performs sparse policy selection, error-type targeting helps by concentrating learning signal on the most valuable decision points — different error types correspond to different decision-point patterns, and the MAB can learn which decision patterns are most improvable. ## Original idea
{
  "title": "Error-Taxonomy-Guided Curriculum for Self-Improving Reasoning via Diagnostic Co-Evolution",
  "core_problem": "Can a PRM serving as a co-evolving diagnostic instrument—classifying step-level reasoning failures into an evolving error taxonomy and feeding a bandit-based curriculum allocator—drive more efficient self-improvement than instance-level weakness targeting (Socratic-Zero), concept-level weakness extraction (SwS), scalar uncertainty targeting (R-Zero), embedding-diversity coverage (Prism), or multi-agent quality filtering (SAGE), and does tracking error-type distribution dynamics across iterations yield predictive signals for convergence and curriculum collapse?",
  "opportunity": "Self-improving reasoning loops have proliferated rapidly, with 25–30 directly relevant papers in the last 12 months alone (ICLR 2026 RSI Workshop accepted 110 papers). Yet despite this activity, every existing framework diagnoses weaknesses at a granularity that is either too coarse or unstructured to support targeted remediation. Socratic-Zero (Sep 2025) achieves +15.4pp via Teacher-generated problems from individual failed solutions but performs instance-level targeting without aggregating error patterns—it cannot detect that 40% of algebra failures stem from sign errors vs. 60% from conceptual gaps. SwS (NeurIPS 2025) achieves 10%/7.7% gains via concept-level weakness identification but conflates distinct failure modes under shared topic labels. R-Zero (ICLR 2026) achieves +6.49 via uncertainty-based co-evolution but its curriculum signal is purely scalar (p̂ ≈ 0.5). SAGE (March 2026) implements 4-agent co-evolution where the Critic scores quality but not error type—it is a filter, not a diagnoser. WarriorMath (Aug 2025) claims 'defect-aware' synthesis but operationalizes defects as binary pass/fail across 16 rollouts. Prism (March 2026) preserves embedding-space diversity but not diagnostic diversity. Meanwhile, the analytical tools exist but remain disconnected from curriculum design: LEMMA (ACL 2025) defines 7 error types for static SFT; Error Classification of LLMs on MWP (EMNLP 2025) discovers 39 dynamic error clusters but uses them only for inference-time prompting; ErrorMap (Jan 2026) builds hierarchical error taxonomies with 95.2% coverage but applies them only for evaluation. The untapped synthesis: use a PRM as a co-evolving diagnostic instrument whose step-level error-type classifications feed a bandit-based curriculum allocator that optimizes learning gain per error category, while tracking error-type distribution dynamics to predict convergence and detect curriculum collapse before it occurs. Two problems may share the same concept (algebra), difficulty level, and even the same error instance pattern yet fail for structurally different reasons (sign propagation error vs. domain restriction oversight)—only error-type-level diagnosis with aggregated statistics can detect these systematic patterns and allocate training resources accordingly. The Self-Evolving Curriculum (SEC, Bengio group, 2025) demonstrates that bandit-based allocation over problem categories yields +13–33% gains over random allocation, but operates on difficulty levels, not error types. Combining MAB allocation with error-type categories would optimize for learning gain per error category—automatically deprioritizing error types that are already being fixed (diminishing returns) or currently too hard (low returns), and upweighting the most learnable weaknesses at each iteration.",
  "landscape": "**Primary co-evolution baselines:** R-Zero (ICLR 2026) achieves +6.49 (Qwen3-4B) via GRPO-trained challenger targeting p̂ = 0.5 uncertainty, but pseudo-label accuracy degrades from 79% to 63% across iterations and the curriculum signal is purely scalar difficulty. Socratic-Zero (arXiv:2509.24726, Sep 2025) achieves +15.4pp (Qwen3-8B) via Teacher-Solver-Generator co-evolution where the Teacher crafts new problems from individual failed solutions using zone-adaptive generation (Gaussian utility centered at 50% success rate); however, it performs instance-level targeting without error taxonomy or step-level diagnosis—it cannot aggregate error patterns across failures or detect systematic weaknesses. SAGE (arXiv:2603.15255, March 2026) implements 4-agent co-evolution (Challenger/Planner/Solver/Critic) with Task-Relative REINFORCE++ achieving +8.9% on LiveCodeBench and +10.7% on OlympiadBench (Qwen-2.5-7B), but the Critic is a quality filter (scores clarity/relevance on a 1–10 scale), not an error diagnoser—weakness detection is purely implicit through difficulty rewards with no error categorization. WarriorMath (arXiv:2508.01245, Aug 2025) implements 'defect-aware' synthesis with a 5-model expert committee and iterative DPO (36.7%→48.3% on AIME'24 across 3 iterations), but operationalizes defects as binary pass/fail across 16 rollouts with no formal error taxonomy despite the title's implication.\n\n**Weakness-driven synthesis (non-co-evolutionary):** SwS (NeurIPS 2025) achieves 10%/7.7% average gains (Qwen2.5-7B/32B) via outcome-level weakness identification → concept extraction → concept recombination → filtered problem generation; single-round, no PRM, cannot distinguish failures sharing the same topic but differing in error pattern.\n\n**Diversity and curriculum:** Prism (March 2026) addresses R-Zero's diversity collapse via embedding-cluster-based rarity bonuses (+3.98 AMC), but diversity is geometric rather than diagnostic. Vocabulary Dropout (April 2026) injects random token-mask diversity (+4.4 avg on Qwen3-8B) but is blind to what kinds of diversity benefit the solver. Self-Evolving Curriculum (SEC, arXiv:2505.14970, Bengio group) formulates curriculum as multi-armed bandit over problem categories, yielding +13–33% over random allocation via learning-gain-optimized selection; operates on difficulty levels, not error types. Cog-DRIFT (arXiv:2604.04767, April 2026) achieves +10.11% on hard problems via format reformulation (MCQ→cloze→open-ended) with instance-level adaptive progression, but reformulates task format rather than targeting error-type-specific content. Bidirectional Curriculum (arXiv:2603.05120, March 2026) simplifies/complicates problems based on pass/fail signals with a multi-agent framework, but adapts difficulty direction without error taxonomy.\n\n**Error taxonomy and diagnosis:** LEMMA (ACL 2025 Findings, arXiv:2503.17439) defines 7 error types (Calculation/Counting/Formula-Confusion/Question-Misinterpretation/Missing-Step/Confusing-Concept/Nonsensical) for error-type-grounded mistake augmentation in static SFT (~89K examples); closest precursor to error-type-driven training but no curriculum, no co-evolution, no RL. Error Classification of LLMs on MWP (EMNLP 2025 Findings, arXiv:2501.15581) discovers 39 dynamic error clusters via K-means on GPT-4o-analyzed failures and applies Error-Aware Prompting (+26.33% on MATH for Llama-3.1-8B), but uses error knowledge only at inference time, not for training or curriculum. Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (arXiv:2602.06795, Feb 2026) derives 234–296 rubric items per domain with keyword clustering (~50% consolidation), achieving +45% over LLM-as-judge baselines; generates rubrics once without iteration or curriculum design. ErrorMap/ErrorAtlas (arXiv:2601.15812, Jan 2026) builds hierarchical error taxonomies via iterative LLM-based clustering with 95.2% coverage and max 25 categories per level, but applies them only for evaluation. PathFinder-PRM (May 2025) achieves SOTA 67.7 PRMScore with error-aware hierarchical supervision (Mathematical/Consistency/Optimality) but does not use error types for curriculum.\n\n**Verifier co-evolution:** CoVerRL (ACL 2026) demonstrates generator-verifier co-evolution with 4.7–5.9% gains but uses undirected majority voting. VHG (arXiv:2605.06660, May 2026) uses verifier-backed three-party self-play (Setter/Solver/Verifier) to prevent reward hacking in problem generation, improving Pass@1 from 56.8% to 69.0%, but optimizes for difficulty without error diagnosis. RL Tango (NeurIPS 2025) co-trains generator and generative verifier via RL but uses outcome-level rewards. Seirenes (May 2026) implements adversarial self-play with evolving distractions (+7.2 to +10.2pp across scales).\n\n**Other related:** DPE (arXiv:2602.22859, Feb 2026) implements diagnose→generate→retrain for multimodal LLMs using 12 coarse capability dimensions with 4 frontier LLMs but without PRM, step-level analysis, or verifier co-evolution. Self-Error-Instruct (ACL 2025) clusters error keyphrases for targeted data generation but uses GPT-4o and doesn't iterate. R-PRM (NJUNLP 2025) achieves best open-source PRM with fine-grained error categories but does not leverage them for curriculum. APRM (Nov 2025) creates adversarial PRM curriculum (+3.4pp solver accuracy) but targets PRM robustness only. 'GRPO is Secretly a PRM' (Sullivan & Koller, arXiv:2509.21154, Sep 2025; under review at ICML 2026) proves GRPO implicitly performs step-level credit assignment via Monte Carlo estimates from shared token prefixes, clarifying that explicit PRMs add unique value as diagnostic instruments rather than reward signals.\n\n**Positioning summary:** No existing work combines: (a) step-level PRM error-type classification, (b) bandit-based learning-gain-optimized allocation across error categories, (c) hybrid mutation+generation problem synthesis with error-type-validated targeting, (d) iterative co-evolution where the diagnostic instrument itself improves, and (e) predictive analysis of error-type distribution dynamics across iterations.",
  "inspired_by": "Socratic-Zero (2025) validates instance-level weakness targeting via Teacher-Solver-Generator co-evolution but without error taxonomy or pattern aggregation; SwS (NeurIPS 2025) validates weakness-driven synthesis but at concept level; R-Zero (ICLR 2026) validates co-evolutionary self-improvement but with scalar uncertainty; SAGE (2026) validates multi-agent co-evolution but with quality filtering rather than error diagnosis; Prism (2026) validates diversity-aware curriculum but with geographic rather than diagnostic diversity; SEC (2025, Bengio group) validates bandit-based curriculum allocation over problem categories but with difficulty levels rather than error types; LEMMA (ACL 2025) validates error-type-grounded training data construction but in a static single-round SFT setting; Error Classification on MWP (EMNLP 2025) validates dynamic error clustering but only for inference-time prompting; ErrorMap (2026) validates iterative taxonomy construction with 95.2% coverage; Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (2026) validates auto-derived error taxonomies with +45% over LLM-as-judge; 'GRPO is Secretly a PRM' (Sullivan & Koller 2025) establishes that GRPO handles implicit credit assignment, clarifying the PRM's unique value as diagnostic instrument. Field guide Gap 7 (iterative self-improvement loops), Gap 4 (dynamic co-evolution).",
  "approach": "We propose Diagnostic Co-Evolution (DiagCoEvo): a framework where a PRM serves as a co-evolving diagnostic instrument whose step-level error-type classifications feed a bandit-based curriculum allocator, while GRPO with standard outcome rewards handles generator training. We initialize generator and PRM from Qwen3-8B.\n\n**PRM Initialization and Cold-Start Strategy.** Rather than directly applying PathFinder-PRM's taxonomy (trained on Mistral traces + PRM800K), which would face distribution shift to Qwen3-8B, we bootstrap the PRM on the target model's own traces: (i) generate 16 solution attempts per problem from Qwen3-8B on a 3K-problem seed bank; (ii) obtain initial step-level labels via consensus of three signals—Monte Carlo correctness estimation, Math-Verify outcome checking, and LLM-as-judge (Qwen3-72B) analysis; (iii) train the PRM on these Qwen3-8B-native traces with PathFinder-PRM's hierarchical error taxonomy as a seed, augmented with data-driven rubric extraction (inspired by Sanders et al. 2026). The initial taxonomy contains five core types: Mathematical-Computation, Logical-Consistency, Conceptual-Gap, Strategy-Selection, Hallucination.\n\n**Taxonomy Expansion Mechanism.** We adopt a concrete expansion protocol inspired by ErrorMap (2026) and TaxoCom (2022): (i) After each DIAGNOSE phase, errors classified with low PRM confidence (softmax < 0.6) are collected into an 'uncertain' pool. (ii) When the uncertain pool exceeds 5% of recent errors, we apply embedding-based novelty detection: compute cosine distance from each uncertain error's representation to all existing category centroids; errors exceeding a Mahalanobis distance threshold (χ² p < 0.01) are flagged as potential novel types. (iii) Flagged errors are clustered (agglomerative clustering with Ward linkage, silhouette-score-optimal k), and clusters with ≥ 20 instances become candidate new categories. (iv) To prevent explosion, we enforce a hard cap of 12 leaf categories and merge categories whose centroid cosine similarity > 0.85 or whose frequency drops below 2% of total errors for two consecutive iterations. (v) Each expansion/merge event is logged for the error dynamics analysis.\n\n**Each co-evolution iteration executes a four-phase cycle:**\n\n(1) DIAGNOSE: The PRM evaluates the generator's solutions on a held-out problem bank (2K problems, 8 solutions each), classifying each incorrect step's error type to produce a weakness distribution w = {w_1, ..., w_K} over error types. We also extract 'error-triggering contexts'—the problem features and reasoning patterns (e.g., nested negation, multi-variable substitution) most frequently associated with each error type via attention-weighted feature extraction from the PRM's intermediate representations.\n\n(2) GENERATE: Hybrid problem synthesis using a three-tier pipeline ordered by reliability. Tier A (Primary—Problem Mutation, ~50% of budget): Take existing problems the model fails on, apply structured mutations targeting the diagnosed error type—constant perturbation, constraint addition/removal, variable relationship alteration (inspired by Arrows of Math). Mutation preserves problem validity better than generation from scratch. Tier B (Secondary—Weakness-Category-Conditioned Generation, ~35% of budget): The generator produces candidate problems conditioned on error-triggering contexts: 'Generate a problem requiring [operation] in a context where [error-triggering pattern] is likely.' This follows SwS's category-conditioned generation but at error-type rather than concept level. Tier C (Tertiary—Fine-Grained Error-Type Generation, ~15% of budget): Direct type-conditioned prompting for the most specific error types, budgeted conservatively given expected 10–25% yield. All tiers pass through error-type-validated rejection sampling: the generator attempts each candidate (8 rollouts per Tier A/B, 12 per Tier C to compensate for lower yield), the PRM diagnoses the solutions, and we retain only candidates where at least one solution triggers the intended error type. ZPD gating (25–75% solvability) filters gradient-vanishing extremes.\n\n(3) TRAIN GENERATOR: GRPO with outcome-level rewards (Math-Verify for answer correctness). Curriculum allocation uses a multi-armed bandit (MAB) over error-type categories, following SEC's formulation: each error type is one arm, reward = |advantage| from GRPO (measuring immediate learning gain), and selection uses Boltzmann policy over Q-values updated via exponential moving average. This automatically upweights the most learnable error types at each stage—deprioritizing types that are nearly solved (diminishing returns) or currently too hard (low returns). A proportional-allocation floor (minimum 5% sampling rate per active category) ensures coverage of rare-but-important error types, preventing the bandit from ignoring them entirely. Standard GRPO handles implicit step-level credit assignment per Sullivan & Koller (2025). We do NOT use explicit PRM rewards for GRPO, cleanly separating the PRM's diagnostic role from the training objective.\n\n(4) UPDATE DIAGNOSTICIAN: The PRM is retrained on the generator's new trajectories, exposing it to novel error patterns at the generator's current capability frontier. This mirrors R-Zero's frozen-partner scheme: during generator training the PRM is frozen; during PRM update the generator is frozen. After PRM update, the taxonomy expansion mechanism runs to detect emergent error types.\n\n**Experimental Design.** We run 5 iterations, tracking three key dynamics: (a) generator accuracy on MATH-500/AMC/AIME, (b) PRM diagnostic quality on ProcessBench/PRMBench, (c) error-type distribution shift per iteration. Our primary analytical contribution is demonstrating that error-type distributions follow predictable phase transitions during co-evolution (e.g., computational errors resolve first, then logical errors, then strategic errors), and that entropy of the error distribution and per-category learning-gain trajectories provide early-warning signals for convergence plateaus and curriculum collapse—enabling principled stopping criteria.\n\nWe compare against five baselines: (i) Socratic-Zero-style instance-level Teacher targeting (closest structural competitor), (ii) R-Zero-style uncertainty-based co-evolution (scalar difficulty, no error types), (iii) SwS-style concept-level weakness synthesis (single round), (iv) R-Zero + Prism diversity preservation (geographic diversity, no error diagnosis), (v) SEC-style MAB over difficulty levels (bandit allocation without error-type diagnosis). Key ablations: (A) error-type MAB vs. proportional allocation vs. uniform allocation (isolates MAB value); (B) hybrid mutation+generation vs. generation-only (isolates mutation value); (C) PRM co-evolution vs. frozen PRM (isolates diagnostician improvement); (D) dynamic taxonomy expansion vs. fixed 5-type taxonomy (isolates expansion value); (E) number of rejection sampling rollouts (8 vs. 12 vs. 16); (F) tiered generation budget ratios.",

# ReasonMaxxer: Key Details from arXiv:2605.06241

## (1) Token Position Impact (1-3%)
The research reveals that RL's effectiveness concentrates on a tiny fraction of positions: "Only 1--3% of token positions are affected, the promoted token always lies within the base model's top-5 alternatives." This suggests RL acts as a surgical intervention rather than wholesale model retraining.

## (2) Probability Mass Redistribution
This phrase means the underlying model possesses solution pathways before RL training begins. Rather than learning novel strategies, RL simply increases the likelihood of choosing paths the model already knew about, essentially reweighting existing capabilities.

## (3) Evidence for Policy Selection vs. Capability Learning
Multiple supporting findings include: the promoted tokens staying within top-5 alternatives (indicating pre-existing knowledge), "targeted corrections at those few positions causally recover a large fraction of RL's accuracy gain, while random corrections fail" (demonstrating specificity), and the base model's entropy naturally identifying these decision points without RL involvement.

## (4) Curriculum Design & Training Implications
The abstract doesn't explicitly discuss curriculum design. However, the sparse intervention model suggests training resources should concentrate on high-entropy decision points rather than distributed capability building.

## (5) Error-Type Targeting
The document doesn't address error-type targeting specifically. The focus remains on decision-point entropy rather than error categorization strategies.

## (6) Benchmarks & Models
Testing spans "three model families, six scales, and six math reasoning benchmarks" but specific names aren't provided in this excerpt.

## (7) Decision Point Value Analysis
No discussion of differential value among decision points appears in the provided content.

## (8) Key Limitations
Limitations aren't explicitly detailed in the abstract provided.

# DARC: Key Details

## (1) Approach
DARC employs a two-stage self-play framework. Stage one trains a Questioner to generate difficulty-calibrated questions using explicit difficulty levels and external corpora. Stage two trains a Solver through asymmetric self-distillation, where a document-augmented teacher creates pseudo-labels for a student Solver lacking document access.

## (2) Achieving +10.9pp Improvement
The framework stabilizes self-evolution by addressing two core instabilities: non-stationary objectives from solver-dependent rewards and bootstrapping errors from self-generated labels. The document-augmented teacher mechanism produces higher-quality supervision, driving the average 10.9-point improvement across benchmarks.

## (3) Decoupled & Asymmetric Design
**Decoupled**: The Questioner and Solver are trained separately with distinct objectives, preventing reward feedback cycles that destabilize optimization. **Asymmetric**: The teacher and student have different capabilities—the teacher accesses external documents while the student doesn't—creating an intentional knowledge gap that improves robustness.

## (4) Curriculum-Based RL Connection
DARC explicitly uses "difficulty-calibrated questions, conditioned on explicit difficulty levels" to structure learning progression, aligning with curriculum learning principles where complexity increases systematically.

## (5) Performance Numbers
Results show "average improvement of 10.9 points across nine reasoning benchmarks and three backbone models" and performance "approaching the performance of fully supervised models without relying on human annotations."

## (6) Key Insights
The framework is model-agnostic, suggesting broad applicability. Decoupling prevents optimization instability while asymmetry enhances label quality—together enabling self-improvement without human supervision.

# SPC: Self-Play Critic Analysis

## (1) Evolution Mechanism for Error Detection

SPC evolves error detection by fine-tuning two model copies in opposing roles: a "sneaky generator" that produces deliberately difficult-to-detect erroneous steps, and a "critic" that evaluates step correctness. These models engage in adversarial competition where reinforcement learning rewards winners and penalizes losers, driving "continuous self-evolution."

## (2) Adversarial Game Structure

The system uses a confrontational game framework where the generator attempts to deceive the critic while the critic identifies errors. This competitive dynamic creates mutual pressure—the generator must craft increasingly subtle mistakes while the critic strengthens its detection capabilities through repeated interactions.

## (3) PRM Co-evolution Relationship

The document doesn't explicitly discuss PRM (Process Reward Model) co-evolution theory. It notes that SPC "surpasses strong baselines, including distilled R1 model" and outperforms "state-of-the-art process reward models," but doesn't theoretically connect SPC to existing PRM evolution frameworks.

## (4) Performance Numbers

- ProcessBench: accuracy improves "from 70.8% to 77.7%"
- Demonstrates significant improvements on MATH500 and AIME2024 mathematical reasoning tasks
- Outperforms contemporary process reward model baselines

## (5) Key Insight

The fundamental insight is that step-level error detection can develop without manual annotations through adversarial self-play, where competitive dynamics naturally calibrate detection sensitivity.

# Actor-Curator: Key Technical Details

## 1. Neural Bandit Architecture

The curator uses a neural network that assigns positive scores to problems: "Cϕ:𝒙↦wϕ​(𝒙)" which implicitly defines a probability distribution "pϕ​(𝒙)≜wϕ​(𝒙)∑𝒙′∈𝒳wϕ​(𝒙′)". The framework operates as online stochastic mirror descent with bandit feedback, balancing exploration-exploitation through entropy regularization.

## 2. Problem Embeddings vs. Categories

The system works directly with **individual problems**, not categories. A two-stage sampling scheme enables scalability: first sampling a candidate batch from a proposal distribution, then the curator reweights within that batch. This avoids requiring explicit problem embeddings or category structures.

## 3. SEC Comparison—Specific Numbers

SEC (Self-Evolving Curriculum) shows these relative differences:
- **Countdown**: Actor-Curator +3.25 absolute (5.52%)
- **ARC-1D**: Actor-Curator +8.50 absolute (30.51%)
- **AIME24**: Actor-Curator +6.67 absolute (28.57%)

## 4. Model Sizes

- **Curator**: Initialized from Qwen3-0.6B; ablations test varying curator sizes
- **Actor**: Qwen2.5-3B (primary), with validation on Llama3.2-3B
- Training uses 30K problems (Countdown, Zebra, ARC-1D) or 12K (MATH/AIME24)

## 5. Training Iterations

Peak performance reported within "the first 100 steps" of training; curves extend beyond this in appendices showing continued improvements.

## 6. Problem vs. Category-Level Performance

The paper doesn't directly compare these approaches experimentally. The system's advantage stems from adapting to "evolving actor training dynamics" rather than static categories, allowing per-problem utility estimates grounded in "policy improvement theory" rather than heuristic bucketing.

## 7. Stated Limitations

"Actor-Curator...gains ultimately depend on the stability and quality of the underlying actor optimization." Additional constraints: requires "reliable reward signal" (best for verifiable domains), introduces "approximately 9% overhead" to wall-clock time, and cannot address "training collapse" alone.

## 8. Error Type Discussion

**No explicit error analysis included.** The paper focuses on aggregate success rates and training dynamics, not error categorization or failure mode distribution.

## 9. OSMD Loss Function

The principled objective combines policy improvement with KL regularization: "ℒcur​(ϕ)=KL​(pϕ∥pt)−η⟨pϕ,𝑼^t⟩". The per-problem utility "u𝒙t" decomposes from the performance difference identity using importance-weighted advantages, providing "actor-aware" credit assignment.

## 10. Non-Stationarity Handling

OSMD explicitly manages non-stationarity via dynamic regret bounds: "RegT≤O​(T2/3​VT1/3)" where VT measures utility drift across iterations. This contrasts with regression approaches that assume stationary targets, enabling adaptation as "the curator adapts to prioritize problems that yield the greatest expected performance gains."

# ReasonMaxxer: Key Findings Analysis

## (1) How RL Affects 1-3% of Token Positions

The paper identifies that RL modifications are sparse and predictable. Table 2 shows only 1.0-4.1% of tokens are "reranked" (where RL prefers a different token than the base model). Critically, "almost zero shifted positions" occur—meaning RL never introduces entirely novel tokens outside the base model's top-5 candidates. The promoted token ranks approximately 2nd among base model alternatives.

## (2) Top-5 Alternatives Finding

This is central to the paper's thesis: "the teacher's preferred token was already a plausible candidate." When RL changes a token choice, it selects from tokens the base model already considers viable. The mean rank of 2.14-2.39 indicates RL acts as a ranker, not an inventor of new reasoning paths.

## (3) Targeted Corrections Experiments

Section 3.2 presents an oracle intervention: replacing base model tokens with RL teacher preferences at disagreement points recovers the teacher's full accuracy using only 1-4% of tokens. Critically, random substitutions fail, establishing causality. This proves specific token choices at decision points drive accuracy gains.

## (4) Implications for Curriculum Design

The edge-of-competence principle emerges: "RL produces genuine gains only at the model's edge of competence, on problems that are difficult but not yet out of reach." ReasonMaxxer exploits this by selecting only problems where base pass rate is between 0 and 1, ensuring both correct and incorrect rollouts exist for contrastive learning.

## (5) Error Types and Diagnostics

The paper distinguishes three token categories:
- **Unshifted**: base and teacher agree
- **Reranked**: teacher promotes a top-5 alternative
- **Shifted**: teacher introduces novel tokens (essentially nonexistent)

Token-level entropy serves as a diagnostic tool—reranked positions show 5-12× higher entropy than unchanged positions, enabling teacher-free decision point identification.

## (6) Benchmarks and Models Tested

**Benchmarks**: MATH-500, GSM8K, AMC 2023, AIME 2024, Minerva Math, OlympiadBench

**Model families**: Qwen2.5 (1.5B-32B), Qwen3 (0.6B-4B), DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B, Mistral-7B

**RL algorithms studied**: GRPO, PPO, RLOO across different baselines

## (7) Key Figures and Tables

- **Figure 1**: Visualizes sparsity and entropy concentration at decision points
- **Table 2**: Quantifies divergence—reranked percentages, entropy ratios, mean ranks
- **Figure 2**: Oracle correction matches RL performance exactly; entropy-gating achieves comparable results
- **Figure 3**: Rank-32 LoRA adapter (0.27-0.49% of parameters) captures full RL correction on MATH-500 and GSM8K
- **Table 3**: ReasonMaxxer matches or exceeds RL baselines at 100-1000× lower cost ($4-25 vs. $200-103,000)

## (8) Are Capability-Specific Training Efforts Futile?

The paper doesn't claim this outright, but suggests reasoning improvement via outcome-only RL is primarily sparse policy selection. The core insight: "RL does not teach new strategies; it redistributes probability mass over solutions the base model already contains." This challenges whether expensive RL infrastructure targets actual capability gaps or merely refines existing knowledge.

## (9) What Makes Certain Decision Points More Learnable?

The paper identifies entropy as the key signal but doesn't deeply analyze *why* specific positions become decision points. It shows that "base-model entropy identifies these positions without any RL-trained model," suggesting entropy thresholds (τ) naturally surface learnable points. The ablation (Figure 4) shows broad robustness across τ values, implying multiple entropy thresholds work—the specific decision point identity matters less than gating strategy.

## (10) Limitations Section

The paper lacks an explicit limitations section. Implied constraints include:
- Focus exclusively on mathematical reasoning with verifiable rewards
- Evaluation on 50-trained problems (smaller data budgets than baselines)
- Single-epoch training approach
- Model-family-specific entropy threshold tuning required
- No analysis of downstream task generalization beyond math benchmarks

---

**Bottom line**: ReasonMaxxer demonstrates that 1-3% of token positions at high-entropy "forks" drive reasoning gains. RL's optimization loop appears unnecessary; contrastive fine-tuning at entropy-gated positions replicates performance with three orders of magnitude less compute.

Actor-Curator is a scalable and fully automated curriculum learning framework for reinforcement learning post-training of large language models (LLMs) that learns a neural curator to dynamically select training problems from large problem banks by directly optimizing for expected policy performance improvement.

The approach formulates problem selection as a non-stationary stochastic bandit problem, derives a principled loss function based on online stochastic mirror descent, and establishes regret guarantees under partial feedback.

Actor-Curator enables effective curriculum learning at scale without human annotations, difficulty labels, or manual dataset structuring, and across diverse reasoning benchmarks—Countdown, Zebra, MATH, AIME, and ARC-1D—it consistently outperforms uniform sampling and strong baselines, achieving up to 30% higher peak performance on ARC-1D and 28% on AIME24.

The search results also show a related approach called "Self-Evolving Curriculum (SEC)" which formulates curriculum selection as a non-stationary Multi-Armed Bandit problem, treating each problem category (e.g., difficulty level or problem type) as an individual arm—this appears to be the category-level approach you mentioned, contrasting with Actor-Curator's problem-level selection.

I found relevant results for your search query. Here's what the research shows about SPaRFT:

## Overview

SPaRFT is a self-paced learning framework that enables efficient learning based on the capability of the model being trained through optimizing which data to use and when.

## Key Components

The framework has two main stages:

1. **Data Reduction with Semantic Clustering**: The approach applies cluster-based data reduction to partition training data by semantics and difficulty, extracting a compact yet diverse subset that reduces redundancy. Each example's feature vector is formed by concatenating its semantic embedding with its difficulty score, and these vectors are clustered into K groups, with representative samples selected to ensure both coverage and diversity.

2. **Multi-Armed Bandit Optimization**: The RFT process is formulated as a Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem, where each arm corresponds to a cluster with similar semantics and difficulty. Thompson Sampling is used to select a cluster at each step, with representative examples fed to the LLM to obtain rewards for RFT, and those rewards used to update the bandit statistics.

## Performance

SPaRFT significantly improves reasoning accuracy and robustness compared to both reinforcement learning and curriculum learning baselines, while reducing the number of training examples by a factor of 100. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks show that SPaRFT achieves comparable or better accuracy than state-of-the-art baselines while using up to 100× fewer samples.

The paper was published in August 2025 and addresses the challenge of making RL-based fine-tuning practical for smaller language models.

Based on the search results, I found highly relevant information about REASONMAXXER and sparse policy selection in RL reasoning:

## Key Findings on REASONMAXXER

REASONMAXXER identifies that RL's beneficial impact is a sparse, predictable correction concentrated at high-entropy decision points where the model is uncertain which branch to take. Only 1-3% of token positions are affected, the promoted token always lies within the base model's top-5 alternatives, and targeted corrections at those few positions causally recover a large fraction of RL's accuracy gain.

These findings reframe reasoning improvement as sparse policy selection, not capability acquisition.

## Token Position Implications

The base model's own entropy identifies these positions without any RL-trained model, and the entire correction is low-dimensional, representable in a tiny fraction of model parameters.

## Threshold Sensitivity and Curriculum

Performance is robust over a broad range: the optimal MATH-500 score (0.50) is achieved at τ = 1.4 (5.2% of tokens), and the optimal GSM8K score (0.72) at the same threshold. A second peak appears at τ = 1.8 (2.6% of tokens) where the decision fraction closely matches RL's observed intervention rate of 2.11%.

REASONMAXXER does not require a precise replication of RL's sparsity; as long as the threshold selects a plausible set of high-entropy positions, the contrastive signal is effective.

The research demonstrates that effective reasoning improvement focuses on sparse policy selection at critical uncertainty points rather than broad capability learning.

# SPC: Self-Play Critic - Detailed Analysis

## (1) Adversarial Self-Play Mechanism
The system employs two competing models: a "sneaky generator" that creates subtle erroneous reasoning steps, and a "critic" that identifies errors. In each game iteration, the generator transforms correct steps into incorrect ones designed to "fool" the critic, while the critic analyzes step correctness. Winners receive +1 rewards; losers receive -1, driving mutual improvement through opposing objectives.

## (2) Reinforcement Learning Algorithm
The approach uses offline RL with importance weighting. The paper states: "we adopt the following optimization objective to achieve efficient and stable RL training" using policy ratio-based updates with KL divergence regularization. The advantage estimation incorporates both rewards and KL penalties to prevent policy drift from initial parameters.

## (3) Generator's Deceptive Error Creation
The sneaky generator undergoes supervised fine-tuning on correct-incorrect step pairs from PRM800K. It "first selects one of the predefined error types and then performs a detailed transformation." The validation criterion requires that original steps achieve ≥75% solver success rate while sneaky variants achieve 0% success rate, ensuring practical impact.

## (4) Critic Improvement Mechanism
The critic initializes using DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B's long reasoning refined into standardized critiques by GPT-4o. Through iterative self-play, it learns from examples where it failed to detect errors generated by increasingly sophisticated generators, progressively enhancing detection capabilities.

## (5) Benchmark Performance

**ProcessBench results:**
- Round 0: 70.8% average accuracy
- Round 1: 76.8%
- Round 2: 77.7%

**PRM800K test set:**
- Round 2: 75.8% average (74.8% correct steps, 76.9% error steps)

**DeltaBench (long CoT generalization):**
- Round 2: 60.5% average with 59.5% harmonic mean

The system outperforms state-of-the-art PRMs including Qwen2.5-Math-7B-PRM800K.

## (6) Error Type Classification
The framework uses "five predefined common error types" for transformation (detailed in appendices). The critic produces naturalistic analyses identifying error categories, though specific type labels aren't enumerated in main results.

## (7) Self-Play Rounds
The paper implements **two rounds of self-play**, employing an asymmetric evolution strategy. Round 1 pairs Sneaky-0 with Critic-0. Round 2 uses Sneaky-1 against Critic-0 to maintain balanced competition (32.5% win rate) rather than synchronous pairing, preventing overfitting.

## (8) Model Sizes
Primary experiments use **Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct** as the base model for both generator and critic. Evaluation solvers include models ranging from 7B to 32B parameters (Llama-3.1, Qwen variants, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B).

## (9) Comparison with Process Reward Models
SPC substantially surpasses traditional PRMs:
- Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B: 62.1% on ProcessBench
- Qwen2.5-Math-7B-PRM800K: 69.7%
- SPC Round 2: 77.7%

Notably, PRMs trained on short CoT show dramatic degradation on long CoT benchmarks (14.3%-41.3% on DeltaBench), while SPC generalizes effectively.

## (10) Key Limitations
The paper acknowledges potential misuse of the sneaky generator for "producing false and misleading information." Technical constraints include reliance on predetermined error types and training primarily on mathematical reasoning tasks, limiting generalization to other domains. The approach requires extensive data generation through multiple LLM calls, raising computational costs.

Key findings:

1. **Actor-Curator** is indeed a strong challenge. It uses a neural bandit operating on individual problem embeddings (not categories) and outperforms SEC significantly. However, it does NOT do error diagnosis at all - it's purely about optimizing which problems to train on. The key question is whether error-type categories provide advantages that problem-level curation misses.

Arguments for error-type categories over problem-level:
- **Transfer**: If you identify that sign errors are a problem in algebra, fixing them also helps with sign errors in calculus. 
- **Interpretability**: Error-type distributions provide interpretable signals for convergence analysis
- **Generalization**: Error types generalize to new problems not in the training bank
- **Analytical contribution**: Error dynamics analysis requires error-type infrastructure
- **Problem generation**: Error types enable targeted problem synthesis (Actor-Curator selects FROM a fixed bank, doesn't generate new problems)

But I should also acknowledge Actor-Curator's strength and consider adding it as a baseline. Actually, Actor-Curator and DiagCoEvo are solving partially different problems: Actor-Curator is about selection from a fixed bank, while DiagCoEvo is about both generation and selection.

Looking at REASONMAXXER's results, the RL signal only affects 1-3% of token positions within top-5 alternatives, which actually supports the error-type targeting approach. If RL operates through sparse policy selection at high-entropy decision points, then different error types map to different patterns of those decision points, and targeting by error type concentrates training on the most improvable decision-point patterns. This reframes the MAB over error types as learning which decision-point patterns need the most redistribution.

SPC is highly relevant here too—it uses adversarial self-play with five predefined error types for step-level error detection and achieves 77.7% on ProcessBench, which validates the error-type approach for PRM training.

I found relevant research on sparse policy selection in RL reasoning. Here are the key findings:

## Sparse Policy Selection in LLM Reasoning

RL's beneficial footprint is a sparse, predictable correction concentrated at high-entropy decision points where the model is uncertain which branch to take. More specifically, only 1–3% of token positions are affected, the promoted token always lies within the base model's top alternatives.

## Key Insight on RL Mechanism

Reinforcement learning does not teach new strategies; it redistributes probability mass over solutions the base model already contains. This means RL does not introduce novel tokens; it consistently elevates one of the base model's top alternatives at moments of uncertainty.

## Curriculum Design Implications

Several recent approaches address curriculum design for RL reasoning:

- Self-Evolving Curriculum (SEC) formulates curriculum selection as a non-stationary Multi-Armed Bandit problem, treating each problem category as an individual arm.

- Goldilocks proposes a teacher-driven data sampling strategy where the teacher model selects questions of appropriate difficulty—neither too easy nor too hard—while training the student with GRPO.

- In sparse reward settings, methods frequently encounter a "cold start" problem where the model fails to discover any successful answers, and HAPO addresses this by introducing the Synthetic Success Injection operator to anchor optimization during failure modes.

These findings suggest that curriculum design should focus on selecting problems that match the model's learning progress rather than simply ordering by difficulty.

# Hide and Seek Game (HSG): Detailed Analysis

## (1) Adversarial Co-evolution Mechanism

HSG operates through two competing roles that improve simultaneously:

- **Sneaky (𝖲)**: Generates incorrect answers with subtle, deceptive errors, rewarded for creating mistakes that evade detection
- **Diagnosis (𝖣)**: Identifies errors and produces diagnostic reports, improving detection strategies through adversarial feedback

The framework uses "dynamic adversarial relationship between error generation and diagnosis, enabling the evolution of challenging errors tailored to the diagnostic role's capabilities." Training alternates between both roles using reinforcement learning with correction success rates as quantitative feedback signals.

## (2) Error Type Classification

The paper identifies two problematic error categories that HSG avoids:

- **Type A (Result Shift)**: "The reasoning is correct, but the final answer differs from the reference"
- **Type B (Explicit Contamination)**: "The reasoning includes clear hints or explicit mistakes that are easy to spot"

HSG successfully avoids both types—92.6% of generated answers contain neither, compared to only 5.4% for competing methods.

## (3) Models Evaluated

- Qwen3-4B, 8B, 14B (primary base model: 4B)
- DeepSeek V3-0324 (685B-parameter MoE)
- GPT-4o (multimodal model)

## (4) Performance Benchmarks

On three mathematical reasoning datasets:

| Dataset | Improvement Range |
|---------|------------------|
| GSM8K | 16.8%–31.4% higher accuracy |
| MATH Dataset | Similar improvements |
| NuminaMATH-TIR | Consistent gains across models |

Specific example (Qwen3-4B): correction accuracy improved from 42.44% to 66.15% (↑23.71%).

## (5) Diagnostic Component Function

𝖣 compares reference answers against erroneous ones, producing reports identifying mistakes. The paper notes this component receives "collaborative feedback" combining diagnostic correctness with whether diagnosis "enables successful correction," promoting "accurate and well-structured reports."

## (6) Training Duration

The paper specifies "600 steps" of training on the combined dataset, conducted on four A800 GPUs.

## (7) Key Limitations

The paper provides no explicit limitation discussion but implies:
- Focus limited to mathematical reasoning tasks
- Future work mentions extending "to broader open-domain and complex reasoning tasks"
- No analysis of computational costs relative to baseline methods

## (8) Comparison with Process Reward Models (PRMs)

**None provided.** The paper compares against:
- LLM-rater Adv+RL (adversarial reward approach)
- RL-only baseline (ablation)

No process reward model comparisons appear in the document.

Based on the search results, I found the paper on arXiv 2601.13761. Here are the key performance details:

## DARC: Decoupled Asymmetric Reasoning Curriculum for LLM Evolution

**Framework Overview:**
DARC (Decoupled Asymmetric Reasoning Curriculum) is a two-stage framework that stabilizes the self-evolution process. The first stage trains the Questioner to synthesize difficulty-calibrated questions, conditioned on explicit difficulty levels and external corpora. The second stage trains the Solver with an asymmetric self-distillation mechanism, where a document-augmented teacher generates high-quality pseudo-labels to supervise the student Solver that lacks document access.

**Performance Results:**
DARC yields an average improvement of 10.9 points across nine reasoning benchmarks and three backbone models. DARC consistently outperforms all baselines and approaches the performance of fully supervised models without relying on human annotations.

**Problem Addressed:**
Existing self-play frameworks often suffer from optimization instability, due to non-stationary objectives induced by solver-dependent reward feedback for the Questioner, and bootstrapping errors from self-generated pseudo-labels used to supervise the Solver.

The paper was submitted to arXiv on January 20, 2026, with a revision on January 21, 2026.

# Actor-Curator Analysis: Key Findings

## (1) Problem Selection vs. Generation
Actor-Curator **only selects from a fixed problem bank**. The paper states: "selects training problems at each iteration" from a large collection 𝒳. There is no generation mechanism discussed—the method curates existing problems, not creates new ones.

## (2) Experimental Comparison Table (Table 1)
Key results for Actor-Curator vs. SEC across benchmarks:

| Benchmark | SEC | Actor-Curator | Improvement |
|-----------|-----|---------------|------------|
| Countdown | 58.87 | 62.12 | +5.52% |
| ARC-1D | 27.87 | 36.37 | +30.51% |
| AIME24 | 20.00 | 30.00 | +28.57% |
| MATH500 | 81.00 | 81.00 | -2.41% |

Actor-Curator substantially outperforms SEC on harder benchmarks (arc-hard: +58.97%, zebra-hard: +13.11%).

## (3) Problem-Level vs. Category-Level Performance
The paper doesn't explicitly discuss why problem-level beats category-level. However, it notes that SEC uses "manually defined buckets" while Actor-Curator enables "function-approximation" across large datasets. The implicit advantage: granular, continuous adaptation rather than discrete bucket assignments.

## (4) Acknowledged Limitations
Yes. The paper states: "Actor-Curator inherits standard assumptions from RL-based LLM post-training...best suited to domains with objectively verifiable rewards such as mathematics, logic puzzles, and code." Additionally, it notes that gains "ultimately depend on the stability and quality of the underlying actor optimization."

## (5) Curator Architecture
The curator is a **separate neural network**. Specifically: "initialized from a pretrained Qwen3-0.6B model" and trained independently. It assigns scores to problems: "Cϕ:𝒙↦wϕ(𝒙)" where wϕ produces weights defining a probability distribution.

## (6) Transfer/Generalization Discussion
**Minimal discussion**. The paper trains and evaluates on the same problem domains. It does mention the curator "generalizes across problems" via function approximation, but no explicit out-of-distribution or transfer experiments are reported.

## (7) Problem Bank Size
Clearly specified:
- **30,000 problems** for Countdown, Zebra, and ARC-1D
- **12,000 problems** for MATH500 and AIME24

Actor-Curator (Feb 2026) achieves +28.6% on AIME2024 via learned problem-level curation but cannot generate problems and has no diagnostic capability. The untapped synthesis: use a PRM as a co-evolving diagnostic instrument whose step-level error-type classifications feed a bandit-based generation allocator—determining WHAT TYPES of problems to generate, not just which existing problems to select. Under REASONMAXXER's sparse-policy-selection framework, error types correspond to families of high-entropy decision-fork patterns; the MAB learns which fork-pattern families are most improvable at each iteration. Error-type categories also enable cross-problem transfer (fixing sign errors in algebra helps with sign errors in calculus—a structural pattern that problem-level bandits treat as independent arms) and provide the analytical infrastructure for the first characterization of error-type distribution dynamics across co-evolution iterations.

"landscape": [combine into one string]
**Primary co-evolution baselines:** R-Zero (ICLR 2026) achieves +6.49 (Qwen3-4B) via GRPO-trained challenger targeting p̂ = 0.5 uncertainty, but pseudo-label accuracy degrades from 79% to 63% across iterations and the curriculum signal is purely scalar difficulty. **Other related:** DPE (arXiv:2602.22859, Feb 2026) implements diagnose→generate→retrain for multimodal LLMs using 12 coarse capability dimensions.
